hook: @ControllerAdvice lets you write exception handlers once and have them apply to every controller in your app.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @ControllerAdvice is a Spring annotation that makes an exception-handling class global. Any @ExceptionHandler methods inside it automatically apply to all controllers in the application — no configuration needed.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Without it, you'd catch exceptions in every controller method individually. Each controller would have its own error handling logic, responses would be inconsistent, and you'd have duplicated code everywhere. @ControllerAdvice solves all three problems at once.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @RestControllerAdvice: the REST-specific version — equals @ControllerAdvice plus @ResponseBody, so handler methods return JSON automatically.
@ExceptionHandler inside the advice: each method maps one exception type to a response.
More specific exceptions match first — UserNotFoundException before the generic Exception catch-all.
Return a consistent error DTO — never a raw stack trace.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: A catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) at the bottom of your advice acts as a safety net for unexpected errors. Without it, unhandled exceptions fall through to Spring's default error handling, which returns a less controlled response format.

cap: The standard setup: @RestControllerAdvice class, handlers for each business exception type, a catch-all handler at the bottom, consistent error DTO throughout.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: @ExceptionHandler is what turns an exception into a controlled HTTP response instead of a raw error page.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @ExceptionHandler annotates a method that handles a specific exception type. When that exception propagates out of a controller, Spring intercepts it and calls your handler method instead of letting it crash the request.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The handler method receives the exception as a parameter and returns whatever response you want — typically a ResponseEntity with an error DTO and the appropriate HTTP status code.

beats.label: parts_or_states
beats.content: Scope is critical. @ExceptionHandler inside a @RestController is local — it only catches exceptions from that controller. @ExceptionHandler inside a @ControllerAdvice class is global — it catches from every controller in the app.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: gotcha: If you put @ExceptionHandler inside a @RestController thinking it will catch exceptions from other controllers, it won't. Fresher code sometimes scatters these into individual controllers and then wonders why error handling is inconsistent. Always put them in a dedicated @ControllerAdvice class.

cap: The service layer throws exceptions freely. @ExceptionHandler catches them at the MVC layer. Business logic stays clean, HTTP concerns stay separate.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: A custom exception named ResourceNotFoundException says more about what went wrong than a generic RuntimeException with a string message.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: The pattern is straightforward: extend RuntimeException, give it a meaningful name, throw it from the service layer when something goes wrong, and catch it in @ControllerAdvice to return the right HTTP response.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Extending RuntimeException means unchecked — no forced try-catch at every call site. The exception propagates naturally up to the MVC layer where your @ControllerAdvice catches it. The service method stays clean.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: ResourceNotFoundException: thrown when a findById returns empty — maps to 404.
DuplicateEmailException: thrown when a unique constraint is about to be violated — maps to 409.
InsufficientStockException: business rule violation — maps to 400 or 422.
Include the resource type and ID in the message: 'User with id 42 not found' is actionable.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: production trap: Returning null from a service method when something isn't found forces null checks into every caller. Eventually someone forgets one and you get a NullPointerException with no context in the logs. Throw an exception instead — it carries meaning, it has a stack trace, and @ControllerAdvice handles it cleanly.

cap: Never expose stack traces to clients. The exception message goes in the error response. The full stack trace goes to your logs.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: A consistent error response structure means clients only need to write one error parser for your entire API.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: A good REST API error response has the same JSON structure for every kind of error. The client doesn't have to handle different shapes depending on whether it was a 400 or a 404 or a 500.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: status: the HTTP status code repeated in the body — convenient for client-side logging.
message: human-readable explanation of what went wrong.
timestamp: when the error occurred in ISO-8601 format.
path: the request URI that triggered the error.
errors: a list of field-specific messages for validation failures.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: For validation errors, include a list of which fields failed and why. A message of 'validation failed' with no field detail forces the client to guess what was wrong. A list of 'name: must not be blank' and 'email: invalid format' is actionable.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: Never include a Java stack trace, internal class names, or database error messages in the error response. Stack traces reveal your implementation details and are a security risk. The stack trace belongs in your server logs, not in the HTTP response. Interviewers with security awareness specifically ask about this.

cap: RFC 7807 defines a standard Problem Details format for HTTP APIs — worth knowing the name even if your team uses a custom structure.

hook: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler is a base class that already handles the standard Spring MVC errors — extend it instead of reinventing them.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler is a Spring-provided base class your @ControllerAdvice can extend. It already contains @ExceptionHandler methods for all the standard Spring MVC exceptions — with the correct HTTP status codes wired in.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: MethodArgumentNotValidException: @Valid validation failure — 400.
HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException: wrong HTTP method for the URL — 405.
HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException: wrong Content-Type — 415.
MissingServletRequestParameterException: required @RequestParam missing — 400.
NoHandlerFoundException: URL matches no controller — 404.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: You extend this class and override only the methods you want to customize. Then you add your own @ExceptionHandler methods for application-specific exceptions like ResourceNotFoundException. You get the standard handling for free and only write what's specific to your app.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: The override method signature for Spring 6 changed — it now uses HttpStatusCode instead of HttpStatus. If you copy older examples, you'll get a compile error. Always check the exact base class method signature for your Spring version.

cap: Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, override the handlers you want to customize, and add your own handlers below. That's the complete production pattern.
followup_handoff: What standard Spring MVC exceptions does ResponseEntityExceptionHandler handle?

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Exception handling best practices separate the good production code from the code that works in demos but breaks in prod.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: There are five pillars to solid exception handling in a Spring REST API.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Centralize: use @RestControllerAdvice as the single place for all error responses.
Meaningful exceptions: name them after what went wrong — ResourceNotFoundException, DuplicateEmailException — not generic RuntimeException.
Consistent error DTO: same JSON structure for every error type so clients parse reliably.
Correct HTTP codes: 400 for bad input, 404 for not found, 409 for conflicts, 500 for unexpected errors.
Log server-side: use log.error with the exception — the stack trace goes to your logs, never to the client.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The layering principle matters too: the service layer throws domain exceptions that mean something business-wise. The @ControllerAdvice translates them to HTTP. The service never knows about HTTP status codes and the controller never knows about business rules.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: Testing error paths is just as important as testing success paths. A @ControllerAdvice that works for the 404 case but breaks for the 409 case is a production bug waiting to happen. Write MockMvc tests for each exception handler.

cap: If your service layer knows about HTTP status codes, something is wrong. If your controller has business logic in catch blocks, something is wrong.
